Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources gathered. I'll organize them verse by verse.

## 2 Samuel 20 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview / Context

The chapter follows immediately from the quarrel between the men of Israel (the ten northern tribes) and the men of Judah at the end of chapter 19. "The angry altercation between the tribes led, according to the proverb (Proverbs 15:1), to fresh troubles. These foreboded greater disasters than had yet occurred, but were happily arrested in the bud. Although suppressed, they must yet have intensified the tribal jealousies, and have sowed the seed of future dismemberment. So goes on the long catalogue of sorrows, following one after another from David's sin." — Ellicott

---

### v. 1: "Now a worthless man named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, happened to be there, and he blew the ram's horn and shouted: 'We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse's son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!'"

**Traditional Reading:**

- "Worthless man" translates Hebrew *beliyyaal* — "a man of Belial," meaning a wicked, lawless, yokeless man who had cast off the yoke of the law. By NT times the term had become synonymous with Satan (2 Cor. 6:15). — Gill; Precept Austin
- Sheba was "of the family of Becher, the second son of Benjamin, and thus of the stem from which Saul was descended" (ISBE, cited at Precept Austin). Ellicott agrees that most recent commentators take "Bichri" as a patronymic — "the Bichrite," i.e., of the clan of Becher, making Sheba of the same clan as Saul. He was at Gilgal with the representatives of the ten tribes and "took advantage of the dispute just mentioned to renew the rebellion of Absalom." — Ellicott
- Sheba's slogan is built on three principles common to rebels: (1) denying the king's sovereignty ("We have no share in David"), (2) devaluing the king's identity ("the son of Jesse" — emphasizing David's humble farming origins), and (3) deciding to go one's own way ("Every man to his tents"). — Enduring Word
- "Every man to his tents" is an idiom from the Exodus/wandering period meaning "to your homes." It was also the signal of revolt — compare the cry of Jeroboam in 1 Kings 12:16. — Ellicott; Precept Austin
- G. Campbell Morgan: "The story should teach us that popular and plausible catchwords ought to be received and acted upon with great caution… Injustice is never corrected by a yet deeper wrong." — Enduring Word; Precept Austin
- The Complete Biblical Library (cited at Precept Austin) notes: "The quarrel had begun about a mere point of etiquette, and now they cast off God's anointed king."
- Sheba is described as calling the people not to battle but simply to abandon David — "he sends them 'to their tents' rather than mustering them for battle." (IVP Bible Background Commentary, cited at Precept Austin)

---

### v. 2: "So all the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Ellicott observes a complete reversal: "Judah, among whom the rebellion originated, and who had been tardy in returning to their allegiance, were now fierce in their loyalty, while Israel… had become alienated and rebellious."
- The verb for "stayed by" (Hebrew *dabaq*) means to cling, adhere, or "stick like glue" — the same verb used in Genesis 2:24 for a man cleaving to his wife. It conveys loyalty and devotion. — Precept Austin
- Enduring Word notes: "The desertion of the ten tribes was distressing but the loyalty of the men of Judah was wonderful. When others desert or divide it gives a greater opportunity to demonstrate loyalty." F.B. Meyer spiritualizes: "We must cleave to Jesus, in spite of the derision of the multitude… in spite of the rebellion of the flesh… when He seems to rebuff us." — Precept Austin

---

### v. 3: "When David returned to his palace in Jerusalem, he took the ten concubines he had left to care for the palace, and he placed them in a house under guard. He provided for them, but he no longer slept with them. They were confined until the day of their death, living as widows."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Absalom had raped these ten concubines publicly as part of his rebellion (2 Sam. 16:20–23). David set them aside upon his return.
- Gill explains: "partly as a punishment for easily yielding to the lust of Absalom, and partly that they might not be seen, which would bring to remembrance his sin." Yet David provided for them and did not put them to death or divorce them.
- Clarke (cited by Enduring Word): "He could not well divorce them; he could not punish them, as they were not in the transgression; and he could no more be familiar with them because they had been defiled by his son. To have married them to other men might have been dangerous to the state."
- "Living in widowhood" — Ellicott explains this as "the necessary result, under the system of polygamy" or "in widowhood of the living" (i.e., while their husband was living, as the Targum renders it).
- Enduring Word: "The sad fate of David's ten concubines is an example of how our sin often has horrible effects on others. They suffered because of Absalom's sin – and David's sin."
- Precept Austin adds a sharp note: "David seems to respond a bit in the flesh… After all who had left the concubines in Jerusalem? David had. And who had heard… the prophecy by Nathan about his wives (2 Sam. 12:11–12)? David had heard this prophecy." The concubines are described as "collateral damage of David's sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah."

---

### v. 4: "Then the king said to Amasa, 'Summon the men of Judah to come to me within three days, and be here yourself.'"

**Traditional Reading:**

- Amasa was Absalom's former general; David had promised him command of the army (2 Sam. 19:13) as a conciliatory move. Ellicott calls this "an act of very doubtful expediency at this crisis."
- Gill notes this command effectively declared Amasa as general of the army.
- Enduring Word: "David knew that time was of the essence. When Absalom had the chance to quickly crush David, he did not take advantage of the opportunity. David did not want to make the same mistake with Sheba."

---

### v. 5: "So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he took longer than the time allotted him."

**Traditional Reading:**

- The cause of the delay is not specified. Gill offers several possibilities: "whether this was owing to the remissness of Amasa, or the unwillingness of the people to serve under him, who had been Absalom's general in the late rebellion, or not having time sufficient allowed him, is not certain."
- Ellicott suggests a different explanation: "Amasa is met on his return at Gibeon (v. 8). He had therefore gone quite out of the bounds of Judah into Benjamin, and had consumed more time in consequence of exceeding his instructions. The fact suggests great doubt of his fitness for the place David had promised him."
- Enduring Word bluntly states: "Amasa wasn't up to the job David gave him. He was not a completely competent military man."

---

### v. 6: "And David said to Abishai, 'Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, or he will find fortified cities and elude us.'"

**Traditional Reading:**

- David deliberately passes over Joab and addresses Abishai (Joab's brother). Gill notes: "it seems he would have nothing to say to Joab, being displeased with him for slaying Absalom, and having removed him from his posts."
- The phrase "escape us" is textually difficult. Ellicott notes: the English follows the Vulgate; others translate "pluck out our eye" (do us great harm); the LXX reads "overshadow our eye" (cause anxiety or hide where we cannot find him).
- David's urgency reflects good military judgment — "delays in such a case as an insurrection being dangerous, which ought to be nipped in the bud." — Gill

---

### v. 7: "So Joab's men, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men, marched out of Jerusalem in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri."

**Traditional Reading:**

- "Joab's men" were the body of men usually under Joab's immediate command; they would readily follow his brother Abishai. — Ellicott
- The Cherethites and Pelethites were David's personal bodyguard, over whom Benaiah was commander (v. 23). The "mighty men" were an elite corps of heroes (see 2 Sam. 23:8). — Ellicott; Gill
- Josephus says there were six hundred, besides the soldiers at Jerusalem. — Gill

---

### vv. 8–10: "And while they were at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa joined them. Now Joab was dressed in military attire, with a dagger strapped to his belt. And as he stepped forward, he slipped the dagger from its sheath. 'Are you well, my brother?' Joab asked Amasa. And with his right hand Joab grabbed Amasa by the beard to kiss him. Amasa was not on guard against the dagger in Joab's hand, and Joab stabbed him in the stomach and spilled out his intestines on the ground. And Joab did not need to strike him again, for Amasa was dead. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Ellicott explains the mechanics: Joab had a girdle bound round his military coat, with a dagger arranged so that "it might fall out as he advanced. He then picked this up naturally in his left hand, and stretching out his right hand to greet Amasa, his movements gave rise to no suspicion."
- Gill explains: holding the beard with the right hand was a customary affectionate greeting among Eastern peoples. The sword was in Joab's left hand, and Amasa had no suspicion.
- Ellicott notes: "Joab's real motive for murdering Amasa, as for murdering Abner (2 Samuel 3:27), was personal jealousy and ambition."
- Enduring Word: "Joab showed how ruthless he was. He murdered Amasa – the man who replaced him as commander of David's armies – out of both rivalry and concern that Amasa did not genuinely support David."
- The blow was to the abdomen ("fifth rib" in some translations = abdomen). Gill notes the wound was in the same place where Abner struck Asahel (2 Sam. 2:23) and Joab struck Abner (2 Sam. 3:27). Clarke speculates Amasa may not have died immediately — "I have known instances of persons living several hours after their bowels had been shed out." — cited in Enduring Word
- Lange's Commentary notes the sober theological reality: "God the Lord, as king of His people, permits sin to work out its extremest evil consequences, in order to reveal His justice in the punishment of sin by sin."

---

### vv. 11–13: "One of Joab's young men stood near Amasa and said, 'Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab!' But Amasa wallowed in his blood in the middle of the road, and when the man saw that all the troops were stopping there, he dragged the body off the road into a field and threw a garment over it. As soon as Amasa's body was removed from the road, all the men went on with Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Ellicott: "Time was too precious for Joab himself to wait. He must put down the rebellion of Sheba by rapid action, and thereby render himself impregnable in the high office which had been his, and which he had now again usurped." The battle cry "suggested that he had rightly been put to death for his doubtful loyalty."
- The people who stood still were likely "the very people whom Amasa had just been gathering from Judah and Benjamin… naturally overcome and paralysed for the moment at the sight of the great leader whom the king had just promoted wallowing in his blood." — Ellicott
- Gill clarifies: "though the wound was mortal, and of which he died, that as yet there was life in him, and through the pain he was in, and the pangs of death on him, he rolled himself about in his own blood."
- Enduring Word: "For all his ruthless devotion to David, Joab was a true leader. The soldiers naturally followed the commander who had successfully led them many times before."

---

### v. 14: "Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel-beth-maacah and through the entire region of the Berites, who gathered together and followed him."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Abel-beth-maacah was at the extreme north of Israel, near Lake Huleh (modern Abil-el-Kamh). It is called "Abel-maim" ("Abel of waters") in 2 Chronicles 16:4. — Ellicott
- The Berites are "apparently a family, or clan, in the north of Israel, otherwise entirely unknown." — Ellicott
- Gill notes some interpret this as Joab (not Sheba) passing through the tribes gathering forces. The Syriac and Arabic versions and R. Isaiah take this view, but Gill favors Sheba as the subject.

---

### vv. 15–16: "And Joab's troops came and besieged Sheba in Abel-beth-maacah and built a siege ramp against the outer rampart of the city. As all the troops with Joab were battering the wall to topple it, a wise woman called out from the city, 'Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here so that I may speak with him.'"

**Traditional Reading:**

- The siege involved "a bank of earth thrown up, for the better working of such engines to more advantage against the city" — what we would call a siege mound. — Gill
- Ellicott explains: "The 'trench' is the space between the wall of the city and the lower outer wall. When the besiegers had succeeded in planting the mounds for their battering engines in this space they had already gained an important advantage."
- The "wise woman" is unnamed but her conduct demonstrates the title. Enduring Word: "Siege warfare was a terrible ordeal for the citizens of the besieged city, and this wise woman was smart enough to seek a speedy end to the struggle."

---

### vv. 17–19: "'…Are you Joab?' 'I am,' he replied. 'Listen to the words of your servant,' she said. 'I am listening,' he answered. Then the woman said, 'Long ago they used to say, "Seek counsel at Abel," and that is how disputes were settled. I am among the peaceable and faithful in Israel, but you are trying to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the LORD's inheritance?'"

**Traditional Reading:**

- Ellicott gives the simplest explanation: "Abel had become proverbial for its wisdom." An ancient Jewish interpretation (incorporated into the Targum) references Deuteronomy 20:10 — the law requiring an offer of peace before attacking a city. Gill notes this interpretation: "she spake, saying, I remember now what is written in the book of the law, to ask a city first, saying, (will ye make peace?) so shouldest thou have asked of Abel…"
- "A mother in Israel" means a metropolitan city with surrounding villages as "daughters." — Gill; Ellicott
- "The inheritance of the LORD" refers to the land that belongs to Yahweh, which Israel holds in trust. — Gill
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary observes: "A peace-maker is a blessing, both to the victors and the vanquished… Greatly are they to be held in honour, who, by wise words and deeds, avert so great a catastrophe as war, especially that most terrible form of it — civil war."

---

### vv. 20–21: "'Far be it!' Joab declared. 'Far be it from me to swallow up or destroy! That is not the case. But a man named Sheba son of Bichri, from the hill country of Ephraim, has lifted up his hand against the king, against David. Deliver him alone, and I will depart from the city.'"

**Traditional Reading:**

- Joab strongly disclaims wanton destruction. The Speaker's Commentary (cited in Ellicott) describes Joab's character: "Politic, decided, bold, and unscrupulous, but never needlessly cruel or impulsive, or even revengeful. No life is safe that stands in his way, but from policy he never sacrifices the most insignificant life without a purpose."
- Enduring Word: "Joab was a practical man. He had nothing against the city of Abel, only against Sheba. If the people of Abel helped him get Sheba it was all the better."
- "From the hill country of Ephraim" — though Sheba was a Benjamite by birth, his dwelling was likely in Mount Ephraim. — Ellicott

---

### v. 22: "Then the woman went to all the people with her wise counsel, and they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it to Joab. So he blew the ram's horn and his men dispersed from the city, each to his own home. And Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem."

**Traditional Reading:**

- Enduring Word: "Sheba probably thought he was safe within the walls of that city, but no one is safe when they run against God's will. There isn't a wall high enough or strong enough to protect against God and His will."
- John Trapp (cited in Enduring Word) draws a spiritual analogy: "Every man's breast is a city enclosed. Every sin is a traitor that lurketh within those walls. God calleth for Sheba's head, neither hath he any quarrel to us for our person, but for our sin. If we love the head of our traitor above the life of our soul, we shall justly perish in the vengeance."
- F.B. Meyer (cited at StudyLight.org) adds: "Sheba's head saved the city… We cannot be more willing to part with our sin than our merciful God is to withdraw His judgments."
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary notes: "The life of one man is sometimes justly sacrificed to secure the life of many. Sheba had no reason to complain that the citizens of Abel bought their own safety with his head."
- Enduring Word notes that the division between Judah and the northern tribes, unresolved after Sheba's death, would eventually lead to the permanent split of the kingdom after Solomon's reign.

---

### vv. 23–26: David's Administration

**v. 23: "Now Joab was over the whole army of Israel; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites;"**

- Enduring Word: "Though he gained the position through murder, David allowed Joab to take control over the armies of Israel."
- Ellicott notes this is a second summary of David's officers (compare 2 Sam. 8:16–18), marking a later period of the reign. "It is noticeable that Joab still remains commander-in-chief."

**v. 24: "Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder;"**

- Ellicott notes "Adoram was over the tribute" — "The 'tribute' should rather be *the levy*, the forced labour so largely employed by Solomon. It is remarkable that there is no trace of such an office in 2 Samuel 8:16–18… It was a feature of Oriental despotism only introduced towards the close of David's reign."
- Enduring Word translates this as "in charge of revenue."

**v. 25: "Sheva was the scribe; Zadok and Abiathar were priests;"**

- Ellicott notes Sheva is called "Seraiah" in 2 Samuel 8:17. Nearly all the officers are the same as in the earlier list.

**v. 26: "and Ira the Jairite was David's priest."**

- Ellicott: "Ira also the Jairite — He is not mentioned in the other lists of the king's officers." On the office (*cohen*), earlier in David's reign it had been occupied by David's own sons (2 Sam. 8:18), "but the murder of the eldest, the rebellion and death of Absalom, and other disorders in his household had led apparently to a change."
- Clarke (cited in Enduring Word) suggests Ira "was probably a sort of domestic chaplain to the king." Enduring Word adds: "If David – a man after God's heart and the sweet psalmist of Israel – needed help in his devotional life, we should not think ourselves above it."

---

## Denominational Distinctives

Given the few searches available, I found limited explicit denominational debate on this chapter. Most traditions read the narrative similarly. Here is what emerged:

- **Baptist perspective (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, StudyLight.org):** Emphasizes practical lessons: "Learn from these things 1) Acting vindictively against one who has wronged you is liable to beget vindictiveness in return; 2) entrusting a business to one who is not of proven capability will produce embarrassment; 3) right or wrong, the heroes usually have their own way in a matter until they answer to God." — Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary

- **Reformed / Broader Evangelical (Lange's Commentary):** Stresses God's sovereignty working through human sin: "By one bad man the greater part of the nation is seduced into insurrection, after David had erred in looking too much to his own honor at his restoration… The unjustly displaced Joab becomes a second time the saviour and restorer of the theocratic kingdom, striding over the corpse of the murdered ex-traitor to victory." God "permits sin to work out its extremest evil consequences, in order to reveal His justice in the punishment of sin by sin." — Lange's Commentary

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Emphasizes spiritual warfare application: Sheba's rebellion as a picture of sin within the believer's heart. "Every man's breast is a city enclosed. Every sin is a traitor that lurketh within those walls." The loyalty of Judah is held up as a model for loyalty to Christ despite mocking, fleshly rebellion, and seasons when God seems distant.

- **Holiness tradition (Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary, which draws from Bishop Hall and Matthew Henry):** Emphasizes the moral and ethical dimensions — the danger of self-interest, the unreliability of those who serve from selfish motives, and the blessedness of peacemakers. "The unreasoning discontent of the multitude is the opportunity of the selfish and ambitious leader. There are always men quick to take advantage of the passion and ignorance of their fellow creatures."

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

- **NET Bible notes / textual issues:** Ellicott mentions the textual difficulty in v. 6 (the phrase "escape us" — alternatively "pluck out our eye" or "overshadow our eye," following the LXX).
- **IVP Bible Background Commentary (cited at Precept Austin):** Notes that Sheba's declaration "effectively announces withdrawal of support of David's kingship, but it does not indicate support for another king." Sheba "sends them 'to their tents' rather than mustering them for battle." Being a Benjamite, there are possible Saulide links, "but the text does not reveal that element."

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

No results were returned from Catholic or Orthodox sites in the searches performed for this specific chapter. The searches did not yield accessible content from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org on 2 Samuel 20.
